report:
# Integrating Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning into Large Neighbourhood Search for Dense MAPF: an Honest Re-implementation and Evaluation of an LNS2+RL-style Hybrid

## Abstract

We implemented an LNS2+RL-style hybrid for Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) and evaluated it on 28 dense benchmark configurations (7 map families, 4 agent counts each, agent density 0.37–0.80). In the hybrid, a learned decentralised multi-agent policy repairs MAPF-LNS2 neighbourhoods in the early search stage, and prioritised planning (PP) repairs them later.

All LNS-type methods share one numba-compiled substrate. Its planner is an exact backward space-time dynamic programme that returns the same (collisions, arrival-time) lexicographic optimum as space-time A*, at up to 3× lower cost.

The MARL operator is a parameter-shared action-scoring network, trained only on procedurally generated random maps by behaviour cloning followed by PPO. Its observation has 26 per-action features:
- a background-aware soft cost-to-go;
- future occupancy;
- team-mate claims;
- broadcast short-horizon intentions of team-mates (a minimal form of communication).

We compare the hybrid against our MAPF-LNS2, PP with random restarts, PIBT, LaCAM and a pure decentralised MARL (SCRIMP-style) proxy. Every method gets the same CPU-time budget: 10 s on 10×10 maps, 40 s on 25×25 maps and 60 s on 50×50 maps. Every returned solution is checked by an independent validator.

**Main finding (negative).** In our implementation the hybrid did not improve on MAPF-LNS2:
- **Success rate:** 9.7 % vs 13.1 % over 236 paired instances (difference −3.4 points, 95 % bootstrap CI [−6.8, −0.4]).
- **Final number of colliding pairs (CP):** 13 % higher (geometric-mean (CP+1) ratio 1.128, Wilcoxon p = 4·10⁻⁷).
- **Seed noise:** an LNS2 seed-1 control differed from seed 0 by only 1.5 % (p = 0.75).

**Why.** A controlled neighbourhood study (identical states, identical neighbourhoods) shows that the learned MARL repair is worse than PP repair at every stage:
- it leaves more collisions after repair;
- its improvement probability is lower;
- it costs 2–2.5× more per call.

The hypothesised early-stage advantage of MARL appeared only on the 50×50 random maps (local CP after repair 39.3 vs 40.8). That advantage was too small to pay for the extra cost.

**Other baselines.** At these densities Python LaCAM and plain PIBT solved 100 % of empty-map instances, where all LNS variants solved 0 %. On maze, room and warehouse maps, LNS2 was the only method with non-zero success.

We report these outcomes as measured. They do not reproduce the improvement claimed by the original LNS2+RL work, and we discuss the likely reasons (operator quality, Python throughput, network size).

---

## 1. Problem and data

**MAPF.** An instance consists of a 4-connected grid with static obstacles and N agents, each with a distinct start and goal. A solution is one path per agent. Each step either waits or moves to an adjacent free cell, and agents rest at their goals after arrival. There must be no vertex collisions (two agents on one cell at the same time) and no swap collisions (two agents exchanging cells across one step). The search-time objective is CP, the number of colliding agent pairs; the instance is solved when CP = 0. We also report the sum of costs (SoC), the sum of arrival times.

**Data.** Each `.npy` file stores five consecutive arrays: obstacle grid (−1 = obstacle), start-occupancy grid, a cell→agent dictionary, starts (N×2) and goals (N×2), with coordinates in (row, col). We verified all 2,400 instances in `code/check_data.py`, with output in `outputs/data_summary.json`:
- starts are distinct and so are goals;
- no start or goal lies on an obstacle;
- every start/goal pair lies in one connected component.

All 100 instances of `data/maps_60_10_10_0.175` are byte-identical to `random_small/maps_60_10_10_0.175`, so we treat them as a single configuration.

| family | size | agent counts | instances per configuration | agent density (agents / free cells) |

| random_small | 10×10, 17.5 % obstacles | 50, 55, 60, 65 | 100 | 0.53–0.90 |
| random_medium | 25×25, 17.5 % | 312, 344, 375, 406 | 100 | 0.58–0.84 |
| random_large | 50×50, 17.5 % | 1250, 1375, 1500, 1625 | 100 | 0.59–0.81 |
| empty | 25×25 | 453, 469, 484, 500 | 50 | 0.72–0.80 |
| maze | 25×25 (with border) | 125, 141, 156, 172 | 100 | 0.37–0.51 |
| room | 25×25 | 250, 281, 312, 344 | 50 | 0.50–0.68 |
| warehouse | 25×25 | 266, 281, 297, 312 | 100 | 0.60–0.70 |

![maps](images/maps_overview.png)
*Figure 1. One instance per family at its smallest agent count (blue: starts, red ×: goals).*

![density](images/density.png)
*Figure 2. Agent density of the 28 configurations. These are far denser than the usual MovingAI "hard" settings; a density of 0.8 means four of every five free cells hold an agent.*

---

## 2. Methods

All code is in `code/`. The solvers are Python with numba kernels; no C/C++ compiler was available.

![method](images/method.png)
*Figure 3. The LNS2+RL hybrid as implemented.*

### 2.1 Shared substrate (`core.py`, `solver.py`)

**Reservation tables.** The current plan is stored as a time-major array P[t, a] over a horizon T, chosen per instance as T ≈ max(2·d_max, d_max + (H+W)/2 + 30), where d_max is the longest shortest path. The supporting tables are:
- vertex occupancy counts, in both time-major and cell-major layout;
- outgoing-edge counts per (t, cell, direction), used for O(1) swap detection;
- an N×N collision-graph adjacency matrix with degrees.

When a neighbourhood is replanned, collision pairs are detached and re-attached incrementally. Collision partners are found by scanning only the timesteps where the agent's cell is shared.

**Single-agent planner.** This is the most important engineering decision, made after profiling. Space-time A* minimising (collisions, arrival time) lexicographically used 97 % of runtime. At these densities it explores almost the whole reachable (cell, t) space whenever a collision-free path does not exist. We also implemented a soft SIPP (safe intervals with soft obstacles, `core.sipp`). It was valid and matched A* quality within 2.5 %, but cells are occupied about half the time, so the intervals barely compress and it was no faster.

We therefore use an exact backward DP (`core.dp_plan`):
- V[t, v] = min over continuations of (4096·collisions + steps);
- a terminal option at the goal costs the future traffic through the goal;
- the sweep is restricted to the ellipse {v : d(s, v) ≤ t − t₀, d(v, g) ≤ T − t}.

This gives exactly the same optimum as A*: identical collision counts and arrival times on every test call (`code/test_sipp.py`). Measured per-call times were:
- room-250: 1.5 ms (A*: 4.6 ms);
- maze-125: 1.1 ms (A*: 1.4 ms);
- random_large-1250: 11 ms (A*: 15 ms).

The hard-constraint variant (collisions forbidden) is used by PP.

**MAPF-LNS2** (Li et al., AAAI 2022):
- **Initial plan:** soft PP in random order.
- **Neighbourhoods:** ALNS (reaction factor γ = 0.1) over two methods, both of size N = 8:
  - the collision-based neighbourhood (random walk on the collision graph, padded with agents spatially close to the selected paths);
  - the random neighbourhood (sampling ∝ deg + 1).
- **Repair:** sequential soft PP in random order. Each agent minimises (collisions, arrival time) against all other paths.
- **Acceptance:** accept iff CP does not increase; on a tie, SoC must not increase.

The failure-based neighbourhood was not implemented.

Measured throughput (CPU time, 2026-era shared server) was about 1,030 iterations/s on 10×10 maps, 110–190 /s on 25×25 maps and about 8 /s on 50×50 maps. The initial plan on 50×50 maps takes about 15 s.

### 2.2 MARL repair operator (`marl.py`)

The m = 8 neighbourhood agents act simultaneously from t = 0. All other agents follow their fixed current paths, which the neighbourhood agents see as dynamic obstacles.

**Execution.** Each step:
1. Each agent broadcasts a 3-step intention.
2. Agents choose actions in a random sequential order, each seeing the moves already committed this step.
3. A shared network scores the 5 actions from per-action feature vectors (softmax over the valid actions).

**Observation features (26 per action).**
- Distance-to-goal change; background vertex and swap collision at t+1.
- Background occupancy of the target cell at t+2…t+5, free neighbours of the target, local congestion.
- Goal indicator and future traffic through the goal.
- Occupancy along the greedy route.
- Team-mate claim, team-mate swap, team-mate currently on the target.
- Agent-level features: normalised distance, at-goal flag, time, nearby team-mates.
- **Planning-informed features:** the excess collision-to-go and excess time-to-go of the action under the exact background-only soft cost-to-go (backward DP per agent), whether the action is the single-agent optimum, and the current collision-to-go.
- **Communication:** whether undecided team-mates intend to enter the target next step, and whether team-mates intend to pass the target within 2–3 steps.

**Network.** One tanh layer of 32 units scores each action; the critic is a linear read-out of the mean-pooled hidden layer. There are about 900 parameters, implemented in numpy with manual backprop (gradient-checked).

**Window W.** MARL plans the first W steps jointly. An agent that ends the window at its goal stays there; the others are completed by the exact soft DP from (position, W), sequentially as in PP. W = 0 reduces exactly to PP repair.

**Training** (`train_marl.py`, CPU only, about 22 min).
- **Training distribution:** procedurally generated random grids only (sizes 10–25, obstacle density 5–25 %, agent density 0.35–0.8), with LNS states sampled after 0, 30, 150 or 400 LNS2 iterations so that both early and late stages are covered. Maze, room, warehouse and empty maps were never seen, so evaluation on them is zero-shot.
- **Phase 1, BC (240 s):** behaviour cloning of soft-PP repairs by teacher forcing; 875k decisions, 90.3 % action accuracy.
- **Phase 2, PPO (1,100 s):**
  - shaped reward: −0.3 per collision step;
  - terminal reward: −(number of collision partners after the repair) − 0.1·(delay);
  - γ = 0.95, clip 0.2, entropy 0.01;
  - a BC regulariser with weight 0.1;
  - episodes of 8-agent neighbourhoods over the full horizon.
- **Checkpoint selection:** best mean local CP on 60 held-out generated neighbourhoods.

The best held-out local CP was 10.87, against 12.10 after BC and 8.15 for PP repair on the same neighbourhoods (Figure 4).

![training](images/training.png)
*Figure 4. Training curve. PPO improves the BC policy by about 10 %, but the learned repair stays about 33 % worse than PP on held-out generated neighbourhoods.*

**Heuristic control policy.** We built a hand-set linear policy over the same features (`make_heur.py`). It is used to test whether learning adds value.

### 2.3 Hybrid LNS2+RL and switching rules

The LNS loop is the one in Section 2.1, with a controller that chooses MARL or PP repair at each iteration:
- **Rate rule (default):** MARL is used, with every 5th iteration a PP probe. Each operator keeps an exponential moving average (EMA, β = 0.1) of CP reduction and of elapsed time. The controller switches permanently to PP once PP's EMA rate (CP reduction per second) exceeds MARL's, after at least 5 probes.
- **Patience rule:** switch after k = 10 consecutive MARL iterations without improvement.
- **Never switch:** MARL only.
- **Bandit:** ε-greedy (ε = 0.2) over the EMA rates of the two operators, never committing.

The main configuration is the rate rule with W = 8. We chose W = 8 from the neighbourhood study (Section 4.1): full-horizon MARL was far worse. Ablations cover W ∈ {8, 16, full}, the BC-only policy and the heuristic policy.

### 2.4 Baselines

- **PP:** prioritised planning with hard constraints and random restarts (exact hard DP per agent).
- **PIBT** (Okumura et al.): dynamic priorities; an iterative stack implementation, because numba's recursion crashed.
- **LaCAM** (Okumura, AAAI 2023): DFS over configurations with lazy low-level constraints and PIBT as configuration generator. Already-visited configurations are re-inserted into OPEN, but there is no LaCAM* cost refinement. The high level is in Python.
- **Pure MARL:** a SCRIMP-style proxy. All agents run the learned policy with no background and no search; success requires every agent at its goal and CP = 0. It differs from SCRIMP: it has no transformer communication and a much smaller network, and collisions are not blocked by the environment. It was not run on 50×50 maps, where the per-agent DP buffers would need about 3.5 GB.

EECBS was not run: at densities ≥ 0.37, bounded-suboptimal CBS in Python is hopeless within these budgets.

### 2.5 Protocol

**Budgets.** CPU-time budgets (`time.process_time`) of 10 s, 40 s and 60 s for 10×10, 25×25 and 50×50 maps. We switched from wall clock to CPU time after observing that, on the oversubscribed shared server (load average about 100–140 on 152 cores), wall-clock budgets gave the same algorithm up to 2× different iteration counts.

**Instances.** The main methods (LNS2, LNS2+RL, PIBT) were run on the first 16 instances of every random_small configuration, the first 8 of every 25×25 configuration and the first 3 of every 50×50 configuration (236 instances). LaCAM, PP, pure MARL, the seed-1 control and the ablations were run on prefixes of the same instance lists (sizes in the tables).

**Validation and statistics.**
- Every returned solution was re-validated by `validate.py`, an independent pure-numpy checker of start/goal, unit moves, obstacles, and all vertex and swap collisions including agents resting at goals. All 134 reported solutions are valid.
- Paired comparisons use Wilcoxon signed-rank tests on final CP, the geometric mean of (CP+1) ratios, and bootstrap CIs (5,000 resamples) for success-rate differences.
- The neighbourhood study (`nb_study.py`) uses one held-out instance per family. It applies every operator to the same 30 neighbourhoods from the same state, at an early stage (right after the initial plan) and a late stage (after 15 s of LNS2).

All tables and figures are regenerated from the JSONL results by `analyze.py`, `fig_nb.py`, `anytime_ratio.py` and `fig_*.py`.

## 4. Analysis

### 4.1 Neighbourhood (stage) study: is MARL better than PP early?

The study takes one held-out instance per family and 30 neighbourhoods per stage. Each operator is applied to the identical state and neighbourhood, and the state is restored afterwards.

| stage | operator | local CP before | local CP after | P(improve) | P(accept) | ms / repair |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| early | **PP** | 40.6 | **27.4** | **0.78** | **0.85** | **15.7** |
| early | MARL learned, W=8 | 40.6 | 29.3 | 0.69 | 0.74 | 30.0 |

| early | MARL heuristic, W=full | 40.6 | 52.9 | 0.16 | 0.17 | 21.5 |
| late | **PP** | 4.8 | **8.1** | **0.09** | **0.24** | 16.5 |
| late | MARL learned, W=8 | 4.8 | 11.2 | 0.07 | 0.12 | 39.0 |
| late | MARL learned, W=full | 4.8 | 20.3 | 0.00 | 0.01 | 30.0 |

*Table 4. Means over the 7 configurations (`outputs/table_nb_study.csv`). "Local CP" counts the pairs involving neighbourhood agents. Time is wall clock and is dominated by the 50×50 instance.*

![nb](images/nb_study_early.png)
*Figure 8. Early-stage repair quality, improvement probability and cost per family.*

![nbstage](images/nb_study_stage.png)
*Figure 9. Local CP after/before repair, early vs late stage.*

1. **The window matters most.** The only MARL variant that comes close to PP is the short window, W = 8, followed by exact soft-DP completion. This reproduces the G1 observation that full-horizon MARL is much worse. Long decentralised rollouts accumulate collisions that the sequential, globally informed DP avoids.
2. **Early stage.** MARL W=8 is close to PP but worse on 6 of 7 families. On random_large, where states are most congested and neighbourhoods most entangled, it is slightly better: local CP after repair 39.3 vs 40.8, P(improve) 0.83 vs 0.80. On empty maps it ties (24.4 vs 24.3). This is the only evidence in our data for the hypothesis that joint MARL planning helps in the congested early phase.
3. **Late stage.** No operator improves often (P(improve) below 0.1), but MARL is clearly worse: local CP 11.2 vs 8.1. PP is the right late-stage operator, as the hybrid design assumes.
4. **Cost.** MARL W=8 costs 2–2.5× PP per repair. It needs a full background cost-to-go DP per agent, then the rollout, then DP completions for the agents that did not finish; PP needs one pruned DP per agent. So even where MARL quality is comparable, its CP reduction per second is far lower. The rate rule therefore correctly switches to PP after about 1.5 s on average.
5. **Learning vs hand-design.**
   - With identical features and full horizon, the learned policy (43.8) beats the hand-set heuristic (52.9). BC alone (43.6) is about as good as BC+PPO.
   - On generated held-out neighbourhoods, PPO improved BC by about 10 % (12.10 → 10.87).
   - The information gap was the largest lever. Adding the background cost-to-go and intention features cut the BC policy's held-out local CP from 35.6 to 12.1, before any RL.

- **Never switching is by far the worst** (2.8× CP, 0 % success). PP is indispensable in the late stage, which confirms that half of the hybrid's design premise.
- **The rate rule beats the patience rule** (1.13 vs 1.20, with an especially large gap on room maps, 1.09 vs 1.22) and beats the bandit (1.33). The bandit keeps spending 37 % of its iterations on the worse operator.
- **The less MARL is used, the better the result.** The variants statistically indistinguishable from LNS2 (W=16, W=full, heuristic policy) are those whose MARL operator is so poor that the rate rule abandons it within about 0.4–0.6 s. The best "hybrid" is therefore essentially LNS2. In our setting MARL repairs give no measurable benefit at any stage, and spending a few early seconds on them costs about 13 % final CP.

Its only relative strength is on the largest in-distribution maps.

## 5. Discussion

**Why we did not reproduce the claimed benefit.** Three factors interact.

1. **Operator quality.** The premise of LNS2+RL is that, in early congested states, a MARL policy that plans the neighbourhood jointly produces fewer collisions than sequential PP. Our policy is small (about 900 parameters, one hidden layer), uses only one-step intention messages, and was trained for about 22 CPU-minutes. It did not reach PP's per-repair quality except on the 50×50 maps. SCRIMP-class models (transformer communication, millions of parameters, GPU-days of training) are a different regime, so our negative result bounds what a lightweight CPU-trained policy can do, not what MARL can do in general.
2. **Relative cost.** Our PP repair is an exact, heavily optimised DP. Every useful MARL design we found needed the same per-agent cost-to-go computation plus a rollout and completions, so MARL can never be cheaper than PP here. In the original system the trade-off is between a GPU network and a C++ SIPPS. The hybrid can only pay off when MARL's quality advantage exceeds its cost ratio, and in our measurements it never did.
3. **Path dependence.** Even about 1.5 s (about 4 % of the budget) of MARL repairs left a persistent, statistically significant deficit (Table 3). The accepted MARL repairs reduce CP, but apparently into states that PP finds harder to finish.

**What the experiments support.**
- The stage-dependent design is directionally right: MARL repairs degrade far more in late stages than PP does, and switching is essential. Never switching gives 2.8× worse CP.
- Rate-based switching is better than patience-based switching, especially on room maps.
- Giving the policy planning-derived observations (cost-to-go and intentions) is the decisive design choice for MARL repair quality. It roughly tripled the BC policy's repair quality.
- Short windows with search completion are much better than full-horizon decentralised planning.

**Comparison with other baselines.** At densities of 0.6–0.8, configuration-space methods (LaCAM, and even plain PIBT) dominate on open maps. LNS-based methods are the only ones with any success on maze, room and warehouse, and they give roughly 2× lower SoC than LaCAM. No method solved random_large, room, or random_medium beyond 312 agents within the budgets.

---

## 6. Limitations

- **Throughput.** Everything is Python + numba on a shared server. Our LNS2 runs about 8–1,000 iterations per second depending on map size, and the budgets of 10/40/60 s CPU are far below the minutes used in the literature. Absolute success rates are therefore much lower than published C++ numbers and should not be compared with them. We report no numbers from the reference papers as our own.
- **Sample sizes.** Instances per configuration are reduced: 16 for random_small, 8 for 25×25 and 3 for 50×50 in the main comparison; fewer for LaCAM (3), PP (2), pure MARL (2) and the ablations (3–6). Family-level conclusions for the secondary baselines are therefore coarse. The main hybrid-vs-LNS2 comparison (236 paired instances, p = 4·10⁻⁷) is robust.
- **Partial baselines.**
  - LNS2 omits the failure-based neighbourhood.
  - LaCAM has no LaCAM* refinement and a Python high level (about 2k nodes/s).
  - EECBS was not run.
  - The SCRIMP proxy is not SCRIMP.
- **Small policy, short training.** Results may change with larger models, longer training, or neighbourhood sizes other than 8, none of which we explored.
- **Timing.** CPU-time budgets remove most interference from the oversubscribed host, but not cache or memory-bandwidth effects. Repair times in the neighbourhood study are wall-clock.
- **Choice of window.** W = 8 for the main hybrid was chosen from the neighbourhood study, which uses held-out instances (index 50/40) disjoint from the evaluation instances (indices 0–15).
